study.title: Psalm 24 The King of Glory and the People Who seeks it
study.overview: Psalm 24 states that all the earth belongs to the LORD, because he created it and sustains it. From this truth, the psalm raises the decisive question: who can go up to the mount of the LORD and stand before his holiness? The answer highlights moral integrity, sincere devotion and search for the face of God. The end of the psalm depicts, in the form of a liturgical call, the triumphal entrance of the King of Glory: the strong, powerful and victorious LORD. Thus, the text unites creation, holiness and worship, showing that the God who governs the world also dwells among his people and requires purity of those who approach him.

outline.title: The Creator's sovereignty over all the earth
outline.explanation: The first two verses lay the foundation of the psalm: the earth, all that is in it, and all its inhabitants belong to the LORD. This is not only a statement about origin, but also about continuous government. The world is not drifting; it is under the dominion of the Creator, who has established him with order and stability.

outline.title: Who can go up to the mount of the Lord?
outline.explanation: The question about who can stand before God introduces spiritual and ethical criteria. The text responds with clean hands, pure heart, rejection of vanity and refusal of lies. This person receives blessing and righteousness from the God of salvation, being identified as part of the generation that seeks the face of the Lord.

outline.title: The entrance of the King of Glory
outline.explanation: The last verses have a form of call and answer, as a festive proclamation. The doors must be opened to the King of Glory, described as strong, mighty in the war and the LORD of hosts. The psalm ends exalting his majesty and his right to enter and reign.

study.context: The psalm is attributed to David and, in the given notes, is likely linked to the occasion of the conduction of the ark for Zion. This background helps to understand the image of doors that open and solemn entry of the King of Glory. Still, the focus of the text is less on the historical event itself and more in the celebrated theological truth: the God of Israel is the Lord of creation, the Holy One who requires purity and the victorious King who lives among his people.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm presents an integrated vision of God. First, he is the Creator and sovereign over the whole creation; nothing exists outside his possession and government. Second, he is the Holy before whom no one can appear without inner and outer integrity. Holiness here is not only ritual, but moral and relational: clean hands, pure heart, sincerity and rejection of falsehood. Third, he is the King of Glory, whose entry is celebrated in the language of triumph. The confessional readings of the commentators see in this psalm an announcement of the reign of Christ and of his providential and gracious dominion; this is a valid interpretation within the evangelical tradition, but the psalm itself, at its most direct level, exalts the LORD as the King who rules, sanctifies and manifests himself to his people. The text also teaches that true worship is not reduced to external ceremony: whoever seeks the face of God must live in a way consistent with his holiness.

scholarViews.insight: The commentary highlights that the pure hands do not shed blood or hurt relationships between people, and that the pure heart is characterized by sincerity, character force and detachment of oneself.

The note reads the psalm as connected to the kingdom of Jesus Christ, seeing in the final verses an invitation to admit the King of Glory and relating this to the government of Christ over the church.
The comment states that the description of those who seek the face of Jacob should be understood as reference to those who seek God's approval, and that this group is approved by the LORD.

questions: What changes in our worship when we remember that the whole earth belongs to the Lord?
In what practical ways clean hands and pure heart appear in Christian daily life, as well as public religious attitudes?
We open real space for the King of Glory in our lives, or do we just honor him with words?
study.practice: This week, examine your life in the face of the criterion of psalm: sincerity, inner purity, integrity in dealing with people and refusal of any deception. Confess God where there is a contradiction between worship and conduct. Also practice a more conscious worship of the sovereignty of the Lord, recognizing that all that you possess and all that you are belong to him. Finally, when reading the psalm in prayer, ask the King of Glory to enter not only his words, but in the concrete decisions of his routine.
study.uncertainty: Notes suggest a probable occasion for the composition of the psalm, but this cannot be affirmed with certainty only based on the text and the notes provided. There is also, in verse 6, a possible textual question mentioned by Adam Clarke in the handwritten tradition, but it is not possible to check here which form should be preferred beyond the translation presented. The Christological interpretations of the commentators are confessional readings and should not be treated as the only obligatory conclusion of the psalm.
